title: Advocates, regulators both call for reforms at power grid operator PJM
summary: As federal energy officials met Thursday for a daylong conference on PJM Interconnection, Maryland legislators and advocates rallied outside the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to express concerns about the multistate grid operator.
content:
by Mayah Nachman and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters July 24, 2026

by Mayah Nachman and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters July 24, 2026

As federal energy officials met Thursday for a daylong conference on PJM Interconnection, Maryland legislators and advocates rallied outside the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to express concerns about the multistate grid operator.

“PJM has lost sight of who its customers are,” said Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery).

“Every decision they make affects the 67 million ratepayers, yet PJM’s governance is primarily accountable to its market participants, those who have a financial stake in the outcome, not the people who are paying those residential bills,” she told a small crowd outside FERC headquarters.

Inside the packed conference, FERC officials appeared sympathetic to the need for change at PJM, the nation’s largest regional power grid operator, calling for improved transparency, faster decision-making and affordability for customers.

“Frustrations are mounting,” said commission Chair Laura Swett. “Put plainly, market participants have lost confidence in PJM’s decision-making abilities.”

FERC put on the conference in response to growing frustrations over PJM’s governing structure, which lawmakers and advocates say gives unfair voting power to companies, including utilities, that have a financial stake in the outcomes of its decisions.

Maryland lawmakers, and Gov. Wes Moore (D), have been among those pushing for state officials to have a greater say at PJM, as their constituents grapple with ever-increasing utility bills. PJM, the nation’s largest electricity grid, includes all or part of 13 states and the District of Columbia.

Hester, who is leading a bipartisan, multistate coalition of legislators pushing for reform at PJM, was joined Thursday by Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery), Pennsylvania Rep. Joe Webster (D-Montgomery) and environmental advocates.

Fry Hester submitted a proposal on behalf of the coalition, outlining ways in which PJM should overhaul its governing structure. They call for ensuring PJM prioritizes affordability and reliability, formalizing states’ roles in decision making and strengthening transparency. They also recommend creating ways to speed up decision-making process and strengthening board independence and accountability, including by requiring FERC to evaluate PJM using specific performance markers.

Charkoudian said PJM’s slow decision-making process and governance structure have undermined states.

“When we look at each of these areas where states are trying to move policy forward on reliability, on decarbonization and on affordability, and where PJM has overridden our ability to do that, we have to ask the question of who is calling the shots,” Charkoudian said. “The people calling the shots are the folks who have money to make when each of these solutions do not succeed.”

Both Fry Hester and Charkoudian thanked the FERC for convening the conference, with Fry Hester noting that she heard commissioners express views that aligned with the collaborative’s recommendations.

Many of the concerns stem back to an energy auction that PJM held in 2024, which ended with a record clearing price an astounding 800% higher than a year before. The reason was an imbalance between energy supply and energy demand, caused in part by massive amounts of demand projected to come from data centers. The auction increased Maryland customers’ bills by varying amounts, with BGE customers faring the worst, with a $21 monthly increase in 2025.

After the auction, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) sued PJM, backed by Moore, and a January 2025 settlement established a new price cap for the auction, which has been extended several times. Each subsequent auction has hit the cap, and consumers are estimated to have saved tens of billions. At the auction for 2028 and 2029, held earlier this month, PJM also wound up securing less energy from suppliers than it had hoped, leaving it with slimmer energy reserves should an emergency affect the grid.

PJM Interconnection electricity price hits cap again in latest auction

Critics have long complained about PJM’s clogged interconnection queue that keeps new projects from connecting to the grid expeditiously. PJM’s procedures were built for a time when a smaller number of large power plants were coming online. These days, with renewable energy projects like solar, wind and battery storage facilities, a much larger quantity of small projects want to come online.

PJM is governed by a board of managers with nine voting members and the PJM CEO, currently David E. Mills. The members must have expertise in various areas, including corporate leadership and transmission systems, but they cannot have any relationship with or financial stake in a member company.

PJM’s more than 1,000 members include transmission owners, generation owners, electricity distributors and others. Consumer advocates from PJM states are ex officio members with voting rights on certain committees. But otherwise, state leaders have no formal role, though they can participate in stakeholder processes and at the Organization of PJM States, or OPSI.

In a comment document prepared by PJM officials for Thursday’s FERC conference, the grid operator notes that when PJM formed, the states chose not to be members, “so as to not be placed in a position to vote or otherwise opine on matters that may subsequently come before them in their role as state commissioners.”

“More recently, the energy politics in each of the PJM states has become more complex,” reads the document. “Within individual states, PJM may hear from governors, utility commissioners, legislators, consumer advocates and other public officials who each hold diverging views. The range of diverse voices speaking for each of the states can make it difficult for PJM to determine how best to incorporate any given state’s view into its decision-making.”

PJM said it has shown “great deference” to the states, including by agreeing to the settlement establishing a price cap for its auctions.

“PJM is open to discussions around how PJM can enhance opportunities for state participation and better define roles and responsibilities,” the document reads. “But such proposals should be paired with an appropriate level of responsibility and accountability based upon our states’ very important role – especially in maintaining resource adequacy for the region.”
